messages.subject_clean: Is it possible to add a botton in the headerPanel?
messages.body_plain:
Just FYI, you never need to switch from ui.R to index.html; ui.R's capabilities are a superset of index.html.

The widgets in Shiny are, by design, a very very thin layer, meant for you to take them apart and create your own forked versions. Type shiny::downloadButton into your R console and you get this:

> shiny::downloadButton
function (outputId, label = "Download", class = NULL)
{
    tags$a(id = outputId, class = paste(c("btn shiny-download-link",
        class), collapse = " "), href = "", target = "_blank",
        label)
}
<environment: namespace:shiny>

So if the class parameter had not existed on downloadButton, you could just copy out the code and tweak the class yourself.

messages.subject: parallelReactives sketch idea
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

  I have a shiny application to display data.  The data is loaded from a remote server (30s?) and then processed to fix date/time issues and decode json-like data in the rows (15 s).  Then it is run through ggplot (5s each plot).

  Each of these operations takes a long time, and blocks all users of the server.

  Ideally, the latency of these operations would not block the UI, but the UI would be updated when they are done.

  I have used curlMultiPerform to get data in the background, solving that block, but I still need to make the decoding, which is currently done in R, non blocking (asynchronous).

  I am going to start using parallel to fork radar tasks to do some of this work.  However, the code will have to be split into the parallelisable logic - that does NOT contain references to inputs or reactiveValues, and the marshaling logic which does the appropriate writes.

  In the longer run it would be great if this just worked in shiny.  I have investigated the options for 'threading' work in R, and the multicore library seems like a good bet.

  I'm thinking that shiny could just use parallel.  I'm thinking about the following scheme:

  parallelReactive({ ... })

  The parallelReactive body is spawned using the 'parallel' function.

  parallel clones global state, so inputs would be visible.  The question is what to do with updated reactiveValues, and how to deal with plots.

  Plots should be simple enough if reactive values can be made to generate plots.  Note that currently plots are updated both on the input$ data (or reactive values) as well as the hidden inputs for width and height, and DPI

  It's not clear to me how to address plots, but I think you guys probably have a very solid idea.  Can you encapsulate the plot logic so it can be used to write to a reactiveValue instead of the output object?

  Dealing with reactiveValues requires a different solution.

  Parallel at the moment returns the final 'return' value from the child process to the parent, presumably serializing it and sending it across the pipe set-up by parallel from the child to the parent.

  For reactives to completely work the following would need to be true:

  * reads from inputs and reactiveValues need to be recorded and collected by the master
  * writes to reactiveValues need to be recorded (with values) and collected by the master
  * any final value required should also be collected, although since observe does not have a return value as such this seems less important - so unless outputs should also be parallelisable this isn't necessary
  * the parallelized jobs should be monitored asynchronously and when the job finished, all of the above should be combined, and the global reactiveValues and reactive control tables in the master should be updated based upon what happened in the child.
  * any discrepancy between the state used by the reactive and the state when the job has finished before collection should betaken account of to see if the reactive computed a value which isn't needed any more

  Since the master is able to keep track of such reads and changes to inputs and reactiveValues, the child should in theory have this capability too.

  So:
  When a parallel child starts, create an empty log
  So: when a reactiveValue is updated AND we are executing in a parallel child context, update the log with the name of the reactive, the action performed, and the associated values
  When the parallel child is about to return, marshal all these into a single data structure
  When the job finishes, master process shiny polls or otherwise detects the job has finished, and invokes a cleanup handler in the master which performs the above steps.

  It feels to me like shiny already needs to perform most of these things, so it would be a matter of fitting awareness of parallel state into shiny, and handling the cleanup logic.

----

  Joe, Winston, what are your feel ins on this matter?

-Alex

messages.subject: App to evaluate R commands?
messages.body_plain:
Greetings.  I'm just taking my first look at shiny.  I've looked at the examples, and they seem clear enough.  But I set myself the task of writing a simple command loop:

while(TRUE) {
    read a command from the user

    execute the command

    display the results
}

This is with all the latest software, installed on Friday, on Ubuntu 12.04.  I've appended the latest in a long series of iterations.  I think the gist of the problem is that I don't know how to get the R command input as a text string.

Thanks for any hints, help, etc., you can provide.

-- Mike

==== ui.R ====

library(shiny)

# Define UI for R-command application
shinyUI(pageWithSidebar(

# Application title.
headerPanel("Run Some R Code"),

sidebarPanel(
textInput("userInput", "Input an R command:"),

submitButton("Run the command!")

),

mainPanel(
h4("Results:"),

verbatimTextOutput("result")
)
))

==== server,R ====

library(shiny)

# Define server logic required to summarize and view the selected dataset
shinyServer(function(input, output) {

# Run the submitted command

inputCommand <- renderText({
input$userInput

})

output$result <- renderPrint({
nextCommand <- inputCommand
eval(parse(nextCommand()))
})

})

messages.body_plain:
You might want to take at look at rNotebook, an R package that allows you to run R in a browser.

http://ramnathv.github.io/rNotebook/

The online version is wired to OpenCPU instead of Shiny to partly overcome the security concerns that Joe pointed out. There are two modes: R mode and Rmd mode which can be used to run R code or knit an Rmd file.

The offline version is wired to Shiny, and can be run from your computer. There is still a security issue here, and you would need to have some firewalls in place.

This package is still under development and can be installed from its github repo.

Hope this is useful.

Cheers,
Ramnath

messages.subject: Re: Proxy Shiny?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sarven!

>
> What do you mean by proxying the connection at 7070 when you have shiny
> running at 8100? What's the external URL with port in the end?
>

The external url would be http://192.168.0.6:8100 (if a user inside the LAN is using the Shiny App). On the server (192.168.0.6), the WebSocket is listening for activity on the 7070 port. In other words,I issue ::runapp( './', port  = 7070) on the R side. Truthfully, I am not interested in users behind the firewall. I was using the unencrypted proxy for proof of concept. I was not sure that it would be possible to proxy a websocket request. It looks like it is. Ideally, I would like to use the reverse proxy as a way to use Apache or NGINX to do user authentication. I am stuck on making the proxy work with https. The initial request works, the webapp comes up, but it is not interactive. If I have a simple web app consisting of a slider and a data table with one cell and I attempt to display the value of the slide in the cell, the slider and table all get rendered, but moving the slider does nothing (the value does not change in the table). In firefox, the failure is silent. In Opera, the failure is listed as a DOMException. It looks like the fact that the proxy terminates the SSL connection at the NGINX server, but forwards an http:// (ws://) request to the Shiny backend is generating a Cross Domain Exception. I have also tried the same thing with STUNNEL and still have the same issue.

> Would you mind giving a quick how-to for your test above?
>

Sure, where and how would like to me to do so?

> Using Apache, my goal (see my earlier reply) is to take a request like
> http://example.org/foo/bar and send it to shiny server like
> http://localhost:8100/?x=foo&y=bar
>

Shouldn't a rewrite with a reverse proxy work? I will look at your attachment a bit more closely.

> -Sarven
>

-Greg

messages.subject: Re: Shiny server can't find packages when they are requested from a sourced file
messages.subject_clean: Shiny server can't find packages when they are requested from a sourced file
messages.body_plain:
Shiny Server runs as the "shiny" user, so whatever libraries are available to that user is what the R process will have access to.

We run as "shiny" by default for security reasons; if there's a security flaw in one of your apps and it's running as your regular user, then your user would be completely compromised.

If you really want, you can tell Shiny Server to run as your regular user by creating a custom configuration file <http://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/rstudio/shiny-server/blob/master/config.html> and changing the run_as directive.

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Jul 1, 2013 at 11:32 PM, Sarven Capadisli <in...@csarven.ca> wrote:
> On 07/01/2013 11:37 PM, Joe Cheng wrote:
> > Oh, sorry. You're not using Shiny Server, so please disregard the
> > previous question.
>
> If using shiny-server, how would this setup be different?

Shiny Server uses sockjs instead of a "raw" websocket, and it tells the browser to load the sockjs JS library through an http URL. (Or it used to; this bug is fixed in our GitHub repo)

>
> The issue I have is that I run shiny like:
>
> R -e "shiny::runApp('foo')"
>
> which runs on http://localhost:8100/
>
> There is an Apache VirtualHost for example.org <http://example.org> with a reverse proxy:
>
> RewriteRule ^/([^/]*)/([^/]*) ws://localhost:8100/?x=foo&y=bar [P]
>
> When the application tries to start, it is attempting to connect to:
>
> ws://example.org <http://example.org>

That's fine. Cross origin only applies to what the browser sees; and as far as the browser's concerned, localhost:8100 doesn't exist. The page URL is http://example.org and the websocket is at ws://example.org <http://example.org>.

>
> Would it be possible to simply start the shiny application at http://example.org/ instead of http://localhost:8100/ or is that only possible through shiny-server?

That would be an awful idea because it would require you to run as root. You also wouldn't be able to support SSL directly out of the R process.

>
> I tried it through shiny-server in any case with this:
>
> listen 8100;
> server_name localhost;
>
> Keeping Apache settings as is. Still no go.
>
> I'm beginning to doubt that Apache websocket is working properly.

Can you try again but without server_name? server_name looks at the value in the Host header that comes from the browser, so that would be example.org <http://example.org> or something. Better to just leave server_name off altogether unless you actually are running virtual hosts.

I would expect this to work because SockJS knows how to use regular HTTP requests instead of websockets if the latter fails. And since the page is coming up in the first place, it seems regular HTTP requests should work.

However you may need to install shiny-server from github, due to the old bug I mention at the top of this email:
sudo npm install -g https://github.com/rstudio/shiny-server/tarball/master

messages.subject: Re: Proxy Shiny?
messages.body_plain:
Oh, you just want to serve up a single Shiny app directly on the root URL; create the following config file at /etc/shiny-server/shiny-server.conf (replace the value in bold):

run_as shiny;

# The directory where application log files should be written to.
# This directory must exist--it will NOT be automatically created.
log_dir /var/shiny-server/log/;

server {
  listen 3838;

  location / {
    app_dir /path-to-your-appdir;
  }
}

Try slapping this at the top of ui.R:

helpPopup <- function(title, content,
                      placement=c('right', 'top', 'left', 'bottom'),
                      trigger=c('click', 'hover', 'focus', 'manual')) {
  tagList(
    singleton(
      tags$head(
        tags$script("$(\"[data-toggle='popover']\").popover()")
      )
    ),
    tags$a(
      href = "#", class = "btn btn-mini", `data-toggle` = "popover",
      title = title, `data-content` = content, `data-animation` = TRUE,
      `data-placement` = match.arg(placement, several.ok=TRUE)[1],
      `data-trigger` = match.arg(trigger, several.ok=TRUE)[1],

      tags$i(class="icon-question-sign")
    )
  )
}

Then sprinkle helpPopup calls liberally throughout your app :)

Try this (this is just the output of fileInput("fileChoice", "Choose File") ). The idea is that file inputs return a dataframe with each row corresponding to a file uploaded. You have to use the datapath column to get its path and read it.

I had a look at libuv, it looks perfect for this.  So I guess the implementation would involve:

* exposing that functionality through httpuv
* adding shiny mechanisms to access that functionality

-Alex

On Friday, June 28, 2013 12:27:03 PM UTC-7, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> All of those async scenarios are probably best supported in httpuv first (meaning, use libuv's built-in functionality for threading, child processes, IPC, I/O, file monitoring, etc., all natively asynchronously).
>
> I'm not sure what you mean by "coordinating writes to a single file or database for multi-user interaction", if you have a specific example scenario that would help.
>
>

> > >
> > > In general I'm now feeling it would be great to get some of the more profound use cases wrapped up in a standard or example implementation - coordinating writes to a single file or database for multi-user interaction with a core dataset seems pretty important and I'm no idea how it might work in the reactive model.  I'm prepared to be astonished by how elegant it tuns out to be, but right now I'm guessing.
> > >
> > > The solutions above do polling, and I'm looking in another direction at the moment - I want to build asynchrony into shiny by allowing it to spawn jobs using R parallel and system fork/exec, and then get the results back in the following ways:
> > >
> > >   a reactive that triggers when it gets the signal that the child has finished.  Using ... wait?
> > >   a reactive that triggers when a file gets updated (for larger results or ones where R would have to write it back to the FS first anyway (e.g. images)  using select()
> > >   a side reactive that monitors stderr to read progress from long running jobs.  Using select()
> > >
> > > -Alex

messages.body_plain:

messages.subject: rest adaptors
messages.body_plain:
This is somewhat off-topic, but.

I'm trying to write a web-app using shiny against a RESTful API.

The API has an impedance mismatch with my application in a number of ways:

  * some operations are dog slow
  * it fails to supply correct mime types
  * some files require extensive reprocessing in R, which R isn't great at speed-wise

Caching of raw and transformed results could definitely help with this, so I'm considering building a whole new RESTful API which proxies on to the original API, but provides the interface I actually want, plus caching, plus on the wire transcoding.

I have asked stack overflow how to solve this, http://stackoverflow.com/questions/17453989/adapter-proxy-for-restful-apis/17455070#17455070, but the attempt is almost certainly doomed, since such questions inevitably turn into a vi-vs-emacs fest, and moderators (of which I am one) tend to kill them off early.

However, having looked at clojure ring, and squid, which fail to please in various ways, I discovered that node.js http-proxy (https://github.com/nodejitsu/node-http-proxy) pretty much meets my needs.  It's a mature proxy that allows for the introduction of middleware on specific routes, and while I haven't discovered whether it can do stream processing, my guess it that it won't be too hard.

I could simply put the caching into my application, but that would complify the application, force R's serial processing on to a parallel problem, and not be re-usable for other clients.  I also hope that by allowing me and others to build a new, nicer API with demonstrable improvements as an adaptor on the original one will spur improvements in the base API!  It's also easier to test this way.

I'm letting you guys know because I am getting an elegant vibe out of this way of working.

-Alex

messages.subject: Re: Shiny server scoping
messages.body_plain:
Shiny Server starts an R process for each app that all users of that app share (so not unlike when you do runApp locally). However, once the last user of that app goes away, and five seconds elapse without another user connecting, then the R process is stopped and a new one is started.

To answer your specific question, "do I need to ask everyone to close the app before changing anything in the code", the answer for both ui.R and server.R is no. If you change either of these files, when the next request (i.e. user) arrives Shiny notices that the file has changed and re-executes it.

There are cases where you may need to force the app to restart though; if you have a global.R file and modify it, or, if you upgrade a package that is in use by the app. You can force a restart by issuing the shell command "touch restart.txt" in the app directory. The next user to connect will force a fresh R process to start.

I am building a site to teach basic statistics, and would like to have a series of GoogleVis graphs and a table that interact with each other. The start of my page can be found at spark.rstudio.com/scm/resid/ <http://spark.rstudio.com/scm/resid/>

Basically, when you click in one scatter chart, I would like a corresponding point in another chart to be selected (and the data row in a table).  I am currently using getSelection to identify the point selected.  An earlier version of my page (spark.rstudio.com/scm/resid-old/ <http://spark.rstudio.com/scm/resid-old/>) shows that when you select a point, the corresponding point is plotted to another scatter graph (the residual from a regression line).

I have been trying to get setSelection to work, but with out any success.  What I have tried so far is to simply set the 4th row for the table to see if setSelection is working.

jscode <- "table.setSelection([{'row': 4}]);"

Any help would be appreciated.

Thanks,

Allen

These two cases are completely different; we use id="..." vs. name="..." to distinguish between the two. If you use ui.R then you don't have to worry about how we implement this difference; just use checkboxInput for the first case, and checkboxGroupInput for the second. In general, ui.R is going to be easier than index.html, and doesn't suffer any loss of control since ui.R can express arbitrary HTML constructions using R code. See ?tags. messages.body_plain:
I don't think this can work. Not because you can't write the jQuery to load the URL that is served by ui.R--you can--but because when the HTML that is generated by ui.R is loaded into the page, it won't work correctly. It's running from a totally different URL than it is expecting, so none of the relative paths will work (including the one to connect back to the server), and the document's onready event has already fired, which Shiny waits for to initialize all of its controls.

Can you do an iframe instead?

messages.subject: Re: sending RGL output to Shiny (non-interactively)
messages.body_plain:
If showing png to the UI is your question, then here is my solution:

1. Make main_panel a uiOutput that's dynamically created in server.R instead of defining it in ui.R.
2. save png plots to tempdir() and in ui.R, call addResourcePath('plots', tempdir())
3. When generating the main_panel, insert the plots using path as 'plots/[your_plot_file_name.png]'.

My example app is here: http://spark.rstudio.com/yuan/rulefit+/
In the "Model" tab, choose some X's as predictors, and click "Run". You'll see some png's added to a tab in the main panel.

On Monday, March 4, 2013 5:26:47 AM UTC-8, Luca Fenu wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I've been playing with rgl within shiny, and even though I'd like ultimately to implement something analogous to the webGL parser function Jeff Allen has shared in a previous post <https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!searchin/shiny-discuss/rgl/shiny-discuss/VV-vw3VFpj0/bszBuHkgtS8J>, right now I'd be more than happy of just printing out the plot generated and let the user download it through a link. Also, this setup is more amenable to batch programs where I have already setup an optimal visual orientation, and do not need interactivity to adjust/explore.
>
> However, rgl doesn't return the plot the same way other graphics systems do, hence can't insert the code in a downloadHandler() call.
>
> I thought I'd save the plot as a png using rgl.snapshot and show it to the user as part of the UI, if nothing else. However, I am not sure of how to do that, either. I understand this should be possible since reactivePlot itself returns a png to the UI for presentation.
>
> Any suggestion?
>
> Cheers,
>
> > Luca

messages.subject: Musing on synchronising reactives to prevent data leaking from record to record
messages.subject_clean: Musing on synchronising reactives to prevent data leaking from record to record
messages.body_plain:
Reactive forests, pseudo-concurrency, garbage collection, race conditions and selecting required reactive paths

Let's suppose we have a database.  The set of record ids can be selected for in a shiny app (sidebar), and a single record can be viewed in the main view.

The single record can be viewed, edited, and when displayed a process is applied to generate a plot, it that is derived from both global settings and the values in the record.

When edited, the plot is re-generated.

Part 1: map reactive components to parts of the UI

In my simple understanding of a shiny app, the UI elements of the single record view would be inputs e.g. textInput, and outputs either by updateXInput or by renderUI.

The plot would be a reactive output that depends upon the current record values and / or the input values.

A button would write the current input values back to the database.

How do we ensure the current values for a given calculation are all coming from the current record?  If the values are treated as individual reactiveValues then it's easy to imagine that there are at least some intermediate states where the plot calculation consumes stale inputs.

In a simple case, perhaps one record field is not editable in the UI - the record id.

output$myplot <- renderPlot({ plot(record$id) })

and one record field IS editable in the UI:

output$editableField1 <- renderUI({ textInput(editableField1Value,record$field1) })

now the plot function looks like this:

output$myplot <- renderPlot({ plot(f(record$id, input$field1Value) })

When the reactiveValue record is updated, first the UI and the plot are uploaded:

SEND {
  editableField1:<input id="field1Value" value="new value">
  myplot:[ plot derived from new record id and old field 1 ]
}

The the client sends back the new UI value to the host

RECV {
  field1Value: new value
}

Then the plot is executed again, with the correct values

SEND {
  editableField1:<input id="field1Value" value="new value">
  myplot:[ plot derived from new record id and new field 1 ]
}

If the UI is more complex, nesting renderOutput in renderOutput, then this might take several steps and plots to stabilize (or might never stabilize, (seriously))

If this is FAST then this might not be an issue, since there is no data safety issue with occasionally displaying the wrong value.

If it's SLOW then the user might draw the conclusion that record2 was the same as record1.

If the update button is pressed, then what values does it depend upon and write into the database?  If it's pressed in between the send to the client and the updated field1Value from the client, then record 2 will be erased and replaced with some fields form record 1

Now this gets serious!

There doesn't seem to be a way to detect when the UI and internal reactives are synchronized on a single record, certainly not programmatically, and while we might ask the user to simply *wait* for the display to settle down, this 1) might never happen 2) might take a long time, during which it *appears* to be settled, 3) exceptions can cause parts of the UI to never update to the proper value 4) asynchrony (such as my mURL or plannel parallel() ) might mean that part of the UI update later, meanwhile they display the old value.

A related issue is that a reactive has no way to express that it can't produce a result just yet - returning NULL allows the *old* value to propagate up the chain, which is precisely the wrong effect.

---

Part 2: map reactive components to parts of the data

What if we took a different view of reactives - instead of having ONE plot, we have enough plots for every record in the database, but we only show one.  The plot ID is different for each record, and the UI is tabbed or conditionaled to show the correct one.

output$myplot_id1234

In addition, the editor UI is different for each record, being templated upon the recordID

This is an interesting structure, because it represents the implied parallelism of the problem - the whole data structure is mapped (as separate entites) into the reactive graph.  Since R is sequential, we probably only want the currently visible parts of the graph to be 'acted', but if we introduced parallelism, then it becomes an issue of 'priority' rather than selection - perhaps the current and previous records would also be active, allowing for fast movement between records.

output$editableField1_id1234 <- renderUI({ textInput(editableField1Value_id1234,records$id1234$field1) })

This would appear to solve the possibility of cross-record interaction.  However, this complicates the design, slows down the UI (since more of it is renderOutput) and brings up a few questions.

1) If a reactive is not being shown, is it nonetheless calculated.  Is that a good thing?
2) if a record is deleted, do the reactives observers and outputs 'go away' or do they stick around and clog up shiny's arteries?  This starts to feel like the same problem as garbage collection
3) can we have a different design for shiny apps which achieves this effect without the pain of manually creating sets of inputs and outputs for each reactive?

----

Part3: multiplexing the UI on the record

A different approach might be to have an observer for each record and each plot, and the plot switches:

plots <- reactiveValues(
  `id1234`=reactivePlot({ plot(record$id1234$id, inputs$id1234$field1})
)
output$myplot <- renderPlot({ plots[[record$id]] })

This starts to look interesting, except that currently inputs (and outputs) are 'flat', which is to say the first level of branches in inputs are special, and the output object can't even have nested reactives in them.

Also it's fairly clear that any time ANY record value or plot was updated, the plot function would be re-invoked - it would be progressively linked against more and more reactives.

I note that the tab UI has a workaround for this - it deactivates the outputs that it's not currently showing, so they are not invoked.  Perhaps a similar code structure could exist in shiny...

plots <- reactiveValues(
  activePlots = which(records==currentRecord)
  deactivateReactive(reactivePlotCollections[!activePlots])
  return(activateReactive(reactivePlotCollections[activePlots])
)

----

I look forward to your input.

messages.subject: Need help to understand how server and client communicate
messages.subject_clean: Need help to understand how server and client communicate
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

My name is Junghoon Lee, and my friend, his students and myself are developing an R library called RIGHT (R Interactive Graphics via HTml) for interactive visualization using JavaScript and HTML5 canvas. Just to give you some idea about what we are doing, here is a demo video the students created some time ago: http://youtube.googleapis.com/v/thlwjYFC_yY?vq=hd1080;hd=1;autoplay=1; If you are interested, we will be happy to discuss more.

We thought that it would be interesting to make our interactive plots become both input and output to Shiny in order to do something like this:

* An interactive plot contains data (imagine a scatter plot) and an overlaid line representing some model fit
* RIGHT will let users select outliers and hide them
* Shiny refits the model with updated data excluding outliers
* The fitted line is updated

Such a capability can be a nice addition to Shiny since RIGHT can provide rich client side interactivity for visualized data and Shiny can help us perform more interesting computation on the server side.

Can you help us gain some understanding of how Shiny server and client communicate? At the end of the day, RIGHT probably has to send and receive some kind of data frame (array of objects) to and from the Shiny server. We started to look into your code, but any pointers on where to start or a simple example code will be very helpful.

Thank you very much!

Sincerely,
Junghoon Lee

In the meantime I think an easy fix is to set outputOptions(session, xxx, suspendWhenHidden=FALSE) for each of your renderUI outputs. I think the problem is that those select inputs don't actually exist at the time that you try to update them (note that outputs, including renderUI outputs, don't run if they're not visible).

messages.subject_clean: Need help to understand how server and client communicate
messages.body_plain:
Dear Joe,

Thank you so much for your quick response, and it will be my pleasure to talk to you once you return from UseR conference.

Meanwhile, I asked one of our students to do the following since he is working on this project as part of Google Summer of Code <http://www.google-melange.com/gsoc/project/google/gsoc2013/sch8906/49001> (the complete proposal is no longer available for some reason). He has to make some pretty rapid progress.
Create an example where
ui.R uses textInput() (see shiny manual at http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/shiny/shiny.pdf)
server.R simply prints the value out using cat() function (debugging techniques at http://rstudio.github.io/shiny/tutorial/#run-and-debug can be useful)
Look at the created JavaScript code and try to understand how the text is passed to the server. Try to modify the code so that you can pass an object array in JavaScript, like an array of (x, y) values. You may have to encode the data into a string to do this for now.
tableOutput() and renderTable() functions may be some help to learn how to encode the data. See the tutorial at http://rstudio.github.io/shiny/tutorial/#shiny-text.
The key challenge for now is to learn how to communicate an object array of, say, (x,y) value between the client and the server. For the moment, we will completely generate client-side JavaScript code based on what Shiny does.  We will try to create a wrapper to make RIGHT an input/output to Shiny once the prototype works,

Please let me know if you have any suggestions, and wish you a safe trip.

Sincerely,
Junghoon Lee

On Sunday, July 7, 2013 2:27:40 AM UTC-4, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> This is very interesting! I would definitely like to discuss this with you, unfortunately the timing is not great as I'm leaving for the useR conference in a few hours. Let's plan to talk more the week after the conference.
>
>
> On Sat, Jul 6, 2013 at 8:16 PM, <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hello,
> >
> > My name is Junghoon Lee, and my friend, his students and myself are developing an R library called RIGHT (R Interactive Graphics via HTml) for interactive visualization using JavaScript and HTML5 canvas. Just to give you some idea about what we are doing, here is a demo video the students created some time ago: http://youtube.googleapis.com/v/thlwjYFC_yY?vq=hd1080;hd=1;autoplay=1; If you are interested, we will be happy to discuss more.
> >
> > We thought that it would be interesting to make our interactive plots become both input and output to Shiny in order to do something like this:
> >
> > * An interactive plot contains data (imagine a scatter plot) and an overlaid line representing some model fit
> > * RIGHT will let users select outliers and hide them
> > * Shiny refits the model with updated data excluding outliers
> > * The fitted line is updated
> >
> > Such a capability can be a nice addition to Shiny since RIGHT can provide rich client side interactivity for visualized data and Shiny can help us perform more interesting computation on the server side.
> >
> > Can you help us gain some understanding of how Shiny server and client communicate? At the end of the day, RIGHT probably has to send and receive some kind of data frame (array of objects) to and from the Shiny server. We started to look into your code, but any pointers on where to start or a simple example code will be very helpful.

messages.body_plain:
Figuring this out in real time.  Option 1 appears to be correct, not sure why it wasn't working for me before.

# option 1
  output$contents <- renderTable({
      dat()
  })

On Monday, July 8, 2013 12:54:32 PM UTC-4, Jason Dalton wrote:
> I'm a little hung up on accessing data from a custom reactive function.  Here is the function, and four options for accessing the data.  I'm not sure which is correct and I've seen all four used in other examples online...   Any help is greatly appreciated.  loving Shiny BTW.
>
>
>
> # server.R
>
> # read multiple input files from a file picker control called 'files', then append them all together using plyr.
>
>
>  dat <- reactive({
>     fileNames<-input$files[,'datapath']
>     names(fileNames)<-fileNames
>     full_data <- ldply(fileNames, read.table, header=input$header, sep=input$sep)
>     full_data
>   })
>
>
> # Direct the combined data frame to a table output.
>
> # option 1
>   output$contents <- renderTable({
>       dat()
>   })
>
> # option 2
>   output$contents <- renderTable({
>       dat()$full_data
>   })
>
>
> #option 3

messages.subject: Re: Need help to understand how server and client communicate
messages.subject_clean: Need help to understand how server and client communicate
messages.body_plain:
For sending data from client to server, check out Shiny.onInputChange(name, value), where value can be anything that can be translated to JSON.

For sending data from server to client, look at the renderText/renderTable/etc. functions as you suggested; those are for sending things that feel like "the main value of this output"; for sending directives to outputs that are not necessarily their "main" value, you can use session$sendCustomMessage(type, value) in server.R, paired with Shiny.addCustomMessageHandler(type, function(value) { ... }) on the client.

See https://github.com/jcheng5/leaflet-shiny for an extensive example of using both of these techniques.

On Sun, Jul 7, 2013 at 5:32 AM, <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dear Joe,
>
> Thank you so much for your quick response, and it will be my pleasure to talk to you once you return from UseR conference.
>
> Meanwhile, I asked one of our students to do the following since he is working on this project as part of Google Summer of Code <http://www.google-melange.com/gsoc/project/google/gsoc2013/sch8906/49001> (the complete proposal is no longer available for some reason). He has to make some pretty rapid progress.
> Create an example where
> ui.R uses textInput() (see shiny manual at http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/shiny/shiny.pdf)
> server.R simply prints the value out using cat() function (debugging techniques at http://rstudio.github.io/shiny/tutorial/#run-and-debug can be useful)
> Look at the created JavaScript code and try to understand how the text is passed to the server. Try to modify the code so that you can pass an object array in JavaScript, like an array of (x, y) values. You may have to encode the data into a string to do this for now.
> tableOutput() and renderTable() functions may be some help to learn how to encode the data. See the tutorial at http://rstudio.github.io/shiny/tutorial/#shiny-text.
> The key challenge for now is to learn how to communicate an object array of, say, (x,y) value between the client and the server. For the moment, we will completely generate client-side JavaScript code based on what Shiny does.  We will try to create a wrapper to make RIGHT an input/output to Shiny once the prototype works,
>
> Please let me know if you have any suggestions, and wish you a safe trip.
>
> Sincerely,
> Junghoon Lee
>
> On Sunday, July 7, 2013 2:27:40 AM UTC-4, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > This is very interesting! I would definitely like to discuss this with you, unfortunately the timing is not great as I'm leaving for the useR conference in a few hours. Let's plan to talk more the week after the conference.
> >
> >
> > On Sat, Jul 6, 2013 at 8:16 PM, <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hello,
> > >
> > > My name is Junghoon Lee, and my friend, his students and myself are developing an R library called RIGHT (R Interactive Graphics via HTml) for interactive visualization using JavaScript and HTML5 canvas. Just to give you some idea about what we are doing, here is a demo video the students created some time ago: http://youtube.googleapis.com/v/thlwjYFC_yY?vq=hd1080;hd=1;autoplay=1; If you are interested, we will be happy to discuss more.
> > >
> > > We thought that it would be interesting to make our interactive plots become both input and output to Shiny in order to do something like this:
> > >
> > > * An interactive plot contains data (imagine a scatter plot) and an overlaid line representing some model fit
> > > * RIGHT will let users select outliers and hide them
> > > * Shiny refits the model with updated data excluding outliers
> > > * The fitted line is updated
> > >
> > > Such a capability can be a nice addition to Shiny since RIGHT can provide rich client side interactivity for visualized data and Shiny can help us perform more interesting computation on the server side.
> > >
> > > Can you help us gain some understanding of how Shiny server and client communicate? At the end of the day, RIGHT probably has to send and receive some kind of data frame (array of objects) to and from the Shiny server. We started to look into your code, but any pointers on where to start or a simple example code will be very helpful.
> > >
> > > Thank you very much!
> > >
> > > Sincerely,
> > > Junghoon Lee

messages.subject: Re: Musing on synchronising reactives to prevent data leaking from record to record
messages.subject_clean: Musing on synchronising reactives to prevent data leaking from record to record
messages.body_plain:
Thanks as always for your feedback, Alex!

Specific nit-picking pedantry first.​

> A related issue is that a reactive has no way to express that it can't produce a result just yet - returning NULL allows the *old* value to propagate up the chain, which is precisely the wrong effect.

I'm not seeing this behavior. If a reactive expression returns NULL, then its value becomes NULL. In fact there is no way, once a reactive expression has started executing, to say "never mind, just use the existing value".

> 1) If a reactive is not being shown, is it nonetheless calculated.  Is that a good thing?

This also shouldn't be happening. Each output has its own observer; that observer is suspended whenever Shiny detects that its corresponding DOM element is not being displayed (size is 0px-by-0px and it or an ancestor has display:none, I believe). Once an observer is suspended, not only does it not execute (actually it may execute 1 more time after you suspend it, if it was already invalidated before you suspended it) but it doesn't cause any of the reactive expressions it depends on to execute, either.

You can override this behavior with outputOptions(..., suspendWhenHidden=FALSE) but by default that's what should be happening (and it's how tabPanel works, there's nothing specific for tabPanel).

> 2) if a record is deleted, do the reactives observers and outputs 'go away' or do they stick around and clog up shiny's arteries?  This starts to feel like the same problem as garbage collection

Reactive expressions go away if they are no longer referenced by anything. Observers go away if you suspend them and if R considers them ready for garbage collection according to the usual rules. However, outputs are referenced from your Shiny session object; you can overwrite them with a new output which would make the old one eligible for GC (and the old observer is also automatically suspended), but that's not the same as just deleting them. We could easily add a method for deleting outputs (or simply accept output$foo <- NULL, which currently errors).

--

I'm still thinking about whether there's another way to solve the general problem in Part 1 that you outline. It's a really interesting question. It feels like there is a general solution that is lurking just beyond my vision.

Here is my understanding, and please tell me if I'm wrong.

reactive() returns a function. This function will not run unless called. Once this function is called, the returned value will be stored somewhere so that the function can be called again and return the same result without actually running it. All input$xxx values appearing in this function will be made association with this function. If none of these input values change, then the function will only be run once (the first time it was called). If any of these input values change, calling this function will trigger the running of all its code and the new returned result will be stored.

If the above understanding is correct, now my question is, can we manually add more things to input$ so that their change will trigger the function to be rerun? For example, I want to make input$abc <- 1 at the beginning, and use it in this reactive function. Then when I need this function to rerun, I can set input$abc to 2. Is that possible?

messages.subject: Re: tutorial examples not working with internet explorer 9 as default browser.
messages.subject_clean: tutorial examples not working with internet explorer 9 as default browser.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe,

Shiny can certainly add a lot of value for many companies. However, in my experience, IT departments for large corporations will be quite inflexible regarding which browsers (and plug-ins) they support. It also goes without saying that many IT departments will favour Microsoft solutions, basically because their staff will usually have invested heavily into learning about Microsoft products.

For those reasons, I think Shiny would be more widely adopted if it would support IE9 and newer browsers.

Kind regards,
Joachim - Zürich

On Friday, November 9, 2012 1:33:07 AM UTC+1, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> Sorry, I think we forgot to document this--we have serious compatibility issues with IE9 and below. That's a pretty big oversight, we'll try to correct that soon.
> IE8 currently doesn't work with either Shiny running locally, or Shiny server (e.g. our live example apps on the Shiny homepages).
> IE9 currently doesn't work with Shiny running locally, but it does work with Shiny server.
> IE10 should work fine with both versions of Shiny.
> If you can install Chrome Frame <http://www.google.com/chromeframe> for IE (any supported version), then both versions of Shiny will work.
> Please let us know if this is a problem for you, including what version of IE you need support for, and whether it's an option for your users to install a more up-to-date browser. If IE compatibility is really going to stop adoption of Shiny in companies then we would consider tackling the quite significant engineering tasks needed to solve these compatibility issues. But of course that means time we couldn't spend improving the rest of the framework. So we definitely need your feedback to help us prioritize.
>
> (In case you are interested in the technical details, Shiny relies heavily on a feature of HTML5 called Websockets. IE8 and 9 don't support websockets; Microsoft used to have a free plugin for IE9 that enabled websocket support, but they seem to have pulled it down since IE10 was released. Shiny server works around this limitation by using communication platforms from other languages (that isn't available in R) that it translates to/from websocket traffic. That's why IE9 works on Shiny server but not locally. IE8 doesn't even work on Shiny server because of a different, unrelated issue <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/3586749/how-to-get-around-ie8-32k-limit-on-datauri-on-base64-encode>.)
>
> Thanks for the question!

You can't add things to input, but you can create your own input-like object using reactiveValues.

values <- reactiveValues()
values$abc <- 1
def <- reactive({
  values$abc * 2
})

Writing to values$abc will trigger reactivity in anything that reads it, just like input does when it changes.

messages.subject: Re: Musing on synchronising reactives to prevent data leaking from record to record
messages.subject_clean: Musing on synchronising reactives to prevent data leaking from record to record
messages.body_plain:
> Specific nit-picking pedantry first.​
Great!

>
> > A related issue is that a reactive has no way to express that it can't produce a result just yet - returning NULL allows the *old* value to propagate up the chain, which is precisely the wrong effect.
>
> I'm not seeing this behavior. If a reactive expression returns NULL, then its value becomes NULL. In fact there is no way, once a reactive expression has started executing, to say "never mind, just use the existing value".

Yep, you are 100% there.  I am still thinking in shiny 0.1.0 and that's how I learned to cope.

>
> > 1) If a reactive is not being shown, is it nonetheless calculated.  Is that a good thing?
>
> This also shouldn't be happening. Each output has its own observer; that observer is suspended whenever Shiny detects that its corresponding DOM element is not being displayed (size is 0px-by-0px and it or an ancestor has display:none, I believe). Once an observer is suspended, not only does it not execute (actually it may execute 1 more time after you suspend it, if it was already invalidated before you suspended it) but it doesn't cause any of the reactive expressions it depends on to execute, either.

Ah, but once an observer has become associated with a reactive, doesn't it always listen to it?

In the case I describe I have associated the reactive for each and every record with one output.

> > 2) if a record is deleted, do the reactives observers and outputs 'go away' or do they stick around and clog up shiny's arteries?  This starts to feel like the same problem as garbage collection
>
> Reactive expressions go away if they are no longer referenced by anything. Observers go away if you suspend them and if R considers them ready for garbage collection according to the usual rules. However, outputs are referenced from your Shiny session object; you can overwrite them with a new output which would make the old one eligible for GC (and the old observer is also automatically suspended), but that's not the same as just deleting them. We could easily add a method for deleting outputs (or simply accept output$foo <- NULL, which currently errors).

What I'm actually concerned about is a little different from this - it's about load on shiny.  I don't want it to have to search through 1000s of dead reactives to find the behavior I want, and I don't want observers to needlessly save megabytes of output that I'm never going to ask them about again.

>
> I'm still thinking about whether there's another way to solve the general problem in Part 1 that you outline. It's a really interesting question. It feels like there is a general solution that is lurking just beyond my vision.

Awesome.  Sorry for not managing to present my problem in a 1+1 way.

-Alex

messages.body_plain:
You can do that easily by modifying updateSliderInput as shown below. You can use the ... arguments to update any argument that is accepted by sliderInput. This is untested, but I believe it should work without any trouble, since all you are doing is sending along more parameters in the message payload.

updateSliderInput = function(session, inputId, label = NULL, value = NULL, ...){
  message <- dropNulls(list(label=label, value=value, ...))
  session$sendInputMessage(inputId, message)

}

messages.subject: Re: Counter Reactivity
messages.body_plain:
You can achieve what you are seeking with Shiny by passing the parameters as a Query String (see this tutorial here
http://rstudio.github.io/shiny/tutorial/#client-data).

http://example.org/?arg1=foo&arg2=bar&arg3=baz <http://example.org/foo/bar/baz>

I don't think Shiny can server arbitrary pages as it will mess up resource paths.  By going down the queryString route, I think you will still get caching, history and the likes of it.

messages.body_plain:
Hi
i am very interesting by this feature and I modified the files as you suggest. Unfortunately, nothing changes : the command Sys.getenv('USERNAME') in RStudio Server gets an empty string

Any idea to help me ?

thanks

Sam

Le mercredi 20 février 2013 14:29:11 UTC+1, floe a écrit :
> The entered username can be passed to the corresponding R instance by utilizing the AppSpec Object (appSpec instance) located in lib/worker/app-spec.js .
> Inside the httpListener in lib/proxy/http.js (--> last post!) the following authentication code is inserted:
>
> > basic.apply(req, res, function(username) {
> >   router.getAppSpec_p(req, res)
> >   .then(function(appSpec) {
> >     appSpec.settings.loginName = username;
> >   })
> > });
>
> This property of appSpec has to be passed to a newly spawned R process by altering lib/worker/app-worker.js around line 150. At the end of the parameter to "this.$proc.stdin.end", where the stdin ('command line') parameters of the R process are generated, the following line is added:
> > (appSpec.settings.loginName || '') + '\n'
> (Do not forget the additional "+" in the line above.)
>
> Next the new command line parameter has to be added to the R environment. In "./R/SockJSAdapter.R" these parameters are read right at the beginning and are copied to the local R environment. Therefor the "Sys.setenv" function gets a new entry:
> > USERNAME=input[4]
> (Again do not forget to get the "," etc. right.)
>
> Finally the provided username can be used inside the shiny (R) application:
> > Sys.getenv('USERNAME')
>
>  Yet again be aware that this is a crude hack by a highly inexperienced user (in fact I've seen any details about node.js for the first time about 24 ago :)
>
> FloE
>
>
> On Tuesday, February 19, 2013 8:01:24 PM UTC+1, floe wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I have also tried to provide a (simple) authentication to shiny-server applications. Therefore I installed the node.js module "http-auth" using npm (no, it did not work at the first attempt):
> > > npm install http-auth
> >
> > As jphilip, I also manipulated "/usr/lib/node_modules/shiny-server/lib/proxy/http.js".
> > After the the first block of code where all the libraries are loaded I added:
> > > var auth = require('http-auth');
> > > var basic = auth({
> > >     authRealm : "Private area.",
> > >     authList : ['user1:pwd1', 'user2:pwd2']
> > > });
> >
> > The authentication logic is applied directly to the httpListener. Therefore after
> > > this.httpListener = function(req, res) {
> > the following line is inserted:
> > > basic.apply(req, res, function(username) {});
> >
> > After saving and closing the file, the server has to be restarted.
> > Now when loading any site provided by shiny-server, username and password have to be entered.

messages.subject: Re: Shiny Concurrent Access & Feature List
messages.body_plain:
Joe,
   In trying to determine server specifications for hosting Shiny Server, I could use some guidance.  We have a simulator we wish to host that has a business request for up to 30 concurrent users (when the commercial version of Shiny is ready to support this).  Is there a formula, or even a best guess, at scoping HW (CPU #cores, RAM) to meet these kinds of concurrent access numbers?

Thanks,

Michael

On Friday, May 24, 2013 4:23:54 PM UTC-4, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:

> Hi Michael, great questions.
>
> On Fri, May 24, 2013 at 8:50 AM, Michael Sevast <michael...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > 1) Is concurrency limitation an issue with the beta of Shiny, or is this a limitation with R in general?
> >          If Shiny, will the upcoming commercial version address this?
>
> The issue is that R does not support concurrent execution. We plan to address this in the commercial version of Shiny by launching multiple R processes, up to 1 per user.
>
> > 2) What are the differences between the beta today and the upcoming commercial version?  is there a link to see the upcoming features and/or history of the releases?
>
> There isn't a public feature list. We intend to release a very early version of the commercial server in late June with simple authentication features, multiple R processes per app, and removal of the requirement to run the server as root. (That last feature will be upstreamed to the open source version as well.) Additional features will be in the final 1.0 release, mostly around security, monitoring, and scaling.
>
> > 3) Once the commercial version is available, what will it cost and what will the support model look like?
>
> We don't intend to charge for the preview version. Pricing for the final version and support are both TBD. If you want to contact me off-list I'd be very interested to hear what your needs and budget are.

messages.subject: Re: hr tag
messages.body_plain:
All HTML tags are defined as tags$p(), tags$div(), tags$hr(), etc. Many of common HTML tags are also accesible just by name, such as:
  p()
  div()
  h1()
and so on.

Many other tags aren't exported to be used without `tags$`. This is in part to avoid using up variable/function names (there are a lot of possible HTML tags) and in part to avoid overlapping with existing object names. For example, title() is a function in the base graphics package, and so if Shiny exposed tags$title() as title(), it would create a naming conflict.

If you want to write a lot of HTML, you can use the withTags function - inside of it, everything that can be used as an HTML tag will be. For example, these are equivalent:
  withTags(
    p("text"),
    hr(),
    p("more text")
  )

  # Same effect as:
  tags$p("text"),
  tags$hr(),
  tags$p("more text")

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Shiny Concurrent Access & Feature List
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael.

(Thanks for your patience on this. We're hoping to get this Enterprise version out to users ASAP.)

The good news is that 30 concurrent users will be a very moderate number in terms of the scale
 we want Shiny Server to be able to handle, so I don't think you'll end
up having to push any boundaries in the software there. My suspicion is that the average use case's hardware requirements will be dominated by the Shiny application you're trying to run, rather than anything in Shiny Server. So you should be able to get a pretty accurate benchmark of the resources you'll need by running the Shiny App you've developed locally on your hardware and monitoring things like RAM and CPU utilization of the R process. Keep in mind that R is single-threaded, meaning that one simulation can run on one R process at a time. So to facilitate 30 simultaneous Shiny users, you'd be looking at running 30 of these separate R processes.

(To be clear for others who may read this message: not every use case demands a separate process per concurrent user. For instance, any of the examples that are bundled with Shiny or are discussed in the tutorial are very "lightweight" regarding computation, and can successfully handle dozens of users with only a single R process. This one-process-per-concurrent-user model only applies in computationally heavy scenarios such as running these lengthy simulations.)

Hope that helps!
Jeff

On Wednesday, July 10, 2013 9:43:11 AM UTC-5, Michael Sevast wrote:
> Joe,
>    In trying to determine server specifications for hosting Shiny Server, I could use some guidance.  We have a simulator we wish to host that has a business request for up to 30 concurrent users (when the commercial version of Shiny is ready to support this).  Is there a formula, or even a best guess, at scoping HW (CPU #cores, RAM) to meet these kinds of concurrent access numbers?
>
> Thanks,
> Michael
>
>
> On Friday, May 24, 2013 4:23:54 PM UTC-4, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > Hi Michael, great questions.
> >
> > On Fri, May 24, 2013 at 8:50 AM, Michael Sevast <michael...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > 1) Is concurrency limitation an issue with the beta of Shiny, or is this a limitation with R in general?
> > >          If Shiny, will the upcoming commercial version address this?
> >
> > The issue is that R does not support concurrent execution. We plan to address this in the commercial version of Shiny by launching multiple R processes, up to 1 per user.
> >
> > > 2) What are the differences between the beta today and the upcoming commercial version?  is there a link to see the upcoming features and/or history of the releases?
> >
> > There isn't a public feature list. We intend to release a very early version of the commercial server in late June with simple authentication features, multiple R processes per app, and removal of the requirement to run the server as root. (That last feature will be upstreamed to the open source version as well.) Additional features will be in the final 1.0 release, mostly around security, monitoring, and scaling.
> >
> > > 3) Once the commercial version is available, what will it cost and what will the support model look like?
> >
> > We don't intend to charge for the preview version. Pricing for the final version and support are both TBD. If you want to contact me off-list I'd be very interested to hear what your needs and budget are.

Hi,

I think it is not possible to test this feature in RStudio Server as the environment variable 'USERNAME' is passed by the shiny server (node.js) to the corresponding R process. You won't get this information in another R process.

Perhaps it helps if you print the whole
Sys.getenv()
output in a text field of your shiny application (after logging in etc.)

--
Florian

messages.subject: SQL query in Shiny
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to create a shiny app that will query a sql table based on the text input of a user.  I think I am close but continue to receive an error stating "$ operator is invalid for atomic vectors".  Any help would be appreciated.

UI Code

library(shiny)

shinyUI(pageWithSidebar(

  # Application title
  headerPanel("Stock"),

  sidebarPanel(
    textInput("symbol", "Symbol", ""),

    submitButton(text="Submit")
  ),

 mainPanel(
    plotOutput("ratePlot"))
))

Server Code

library(shiny)
library(RODBC)

dbhandle <- odbcDriverConnect('driver={SQL Server Native Client 10.0};server=ppi-sql9;database=VendorData;trusted_connection=yes')

locate <- sqlQuery(dbhandle,"SELECT [TransDate]
                   ,[UnderlyingSymbol]
                   ,[Rate]
                   FROM [VendorData].[dbo].[tblBorrow]
                   where UnderlyingSymbol=toupper(input$symbol)")

shinyServer(function(input, output) {
  output$ratePlot <- renderPlot({
    data <- locate[locate$UnderlyingSymbol == toupper(input$symbol),]
    if (nrow(data) == 0)
      NULL
    else
      plot(data$Rate)
  })

})

messages.body_plain:
Jeff,
  Thank you for the feedback.  We are looking forward to the release of the Enterprise version to be able to take this to another level :-)

Michael

On Thursday, July 11, 2013 8:33:00 AM UTC-4, Jeff Allen wrote:
> Hi Michael.
>
> (Thanks for your patience on this. We're hoping to get this Enterprise version out to users ASAP.)
>
> The good news is that 30 concurrent users will be a very moderate number in terms of the scale we want Shiny Server to be able to handle, so I don't think you'll end up having to push any boundaries in the software there. My suspicion is that the average use case's hardware requirements will be dominated by the Shiny application you're trying to run, rather than anything in Shiny Server. So you should be able to get a pretty accurate benchmark of the resources you'll need by running the Shiny App you've developed locally on your hardware and monitoring things like RAM and CPU utilization of the R process. Keep in mind that R is single-threaded, meaning that one simulation can run on one R process at a time. So to facilitate 30 simultaneous Shiny users, you'd be looking at running 30 of these separate R processes.
>
> (To be clear for others who may read this message: not every use case demands a separate process per concurrent user. For instance, any of the examples that are bundled with Shiny or are discussed in the tutorial are very "lightweight" regarding computation, and can successfully handle dozens of users with only a single R process. This one-process-per-concurrent-user model only applies in computationally heavy scenarios such as running these lengthy simulations.)
>
> Hope that helps!
> Jeff
>
>
>
> On Wednesday, July 10, 2013 9:43:11 AM UTC-5, Michael Sevast wrote:
> > Joe,
> >    In trying to determine server specifications for hosting Shiny Server, I could use some guidance.  We have a simulator we wish to host that has a business request for up to 30 concurrent users (when the commercial version of Shiny is ready to support this).  Is there a formula, or even a best guess, at scoping HW (CPU #cores, RAM) to meet these kinds of concurrent access numbers?
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Michael
> >
> >
> > On Friday, May 24, 2013 4:23:54 PM UTC-4, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > > Hi Michael, great questions.
> > >
> > > On Fri, May 24, 2013 at 8:50 AM, Michael Sevast <michael...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > 1) Is concurrency limitation an issue with the beta of Shiny, or is this a limitation with R in general?
> > > >          If Shiny, will the upcoming commercial version address this?
> > >
> > > The issue is that R does not support concurrent execution. We plan to address this in the commercial version of Shiny by launching multiple R processes, up to 1 per user.
> > >
> > > > 2) What are the differences between the beta today and the upcoming commercial version?  is there a link to see the upcoming features and/or history of the releases?
> > >
> > > There isn't a public feature list. We intend to release a very early version of the commercial server in late June with simple authentication features, multiple R processes per app, and removal of the requirement to run the server as root. (That last feature will be upstreamed to the open source version as well.) Additional features will be in the final 1.0 release, mostly around security, monitoring, and scaling.
> > >
> > > > 3) Once the commercial version is available, what will it cost and what will the support model look like?
> > >
> > > We don't intend to charge for the preview version. Pricing for the final version and support are both TBD. If you want to contact me off-list I'd be very interested to hear what your needs and budget are.

messages.subject: Re: SQL query in Shiny
messages.body_plain:
well, im assuming the issue is in the query portion and not the output portion (but you may want to check this if you haven't already), so my first guess would be to make reactives from the inputs, and use those in the queries instead, and see if that is a sufficient 'fix',
ie
sym=reactive({
input$symbol

})
locate <- sqlQuery(dbhandle,"SELECT [TransDate]
                   ,[UnderlyingSymbol]
                   ,[Rate]
                   FROM [VendorData].[dbo].[tblBorrow]

                   where UnderlyingSymbol=toupper(sym())")

personally I would consider throwing in an action button in the ui and an isolate in the sym() so it wouldn't do a query each time a letter was typed.  It would also help with debugging, where putting an
if(input$myactionbutton<1)
return()
browser()
would show if the error occurred in the query or in the output.  Hope this helps.

messages.subject: Re: Persistent R sessions in Shiny Server?
messages.subject_clean: Persistent R sessions in Shiny Server?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sarven,

What operating system are you using?

We're aware of a bug in recent Debian systems (Ubuntu 14 included) described here: https://github.com/rstudio/shiny-server/issues/22 . We're working on the fix, but it's going to require a fair amount of work and testing to get it running properly.

Does that sound like it might describe the issue you have?

Jeff

messages.subject: Can you exit from a Shiny app without interrupting R?
messages.subject_clean: Can you exit from a Shiny app without interrupting R?
messages.body_plain:
Apologies if this has been covered or is trivial, but I can't figure it out:

If you start a Shiny app from within a longer R script, is there a way to exit from the Shiny app and continue with the execution of the calling script?

What I am trying to do is 1) load and reformat a large dataset with an R script, 2) do some processing interactively with Shiny (low-pass filtering, baseline adjustment, peak finding), and 3) run the final computations non-interactively. The official way of ending Shiny (http://rstudio.github.io/shiny/tutorial/#run-and-debug) requires interrupting R by typing Esc or clicking Stop, which also terminates the execution of the calling script.

One way around the problem would be writing the reformatted dataset to a temporary file and pause the calling R script; start Shiny as a separate process, load the temp file, do the interactive processing, and write another temp file; and resume the calling script, read in the second temp file, and finish. That's a bit klutzy, and all the file I/O takes a while.

Another way would be doing everything within the Shiny framework. But I don't want the structure of the entire program to depend on a single R package and I want to be able to interact directly with my data from the R console.

Thanks for any help,

Richard

messages.body_plain:
If I understand your problem correctly, I think your best bet is to wrap up your workflow in a normal R script, then interject the Shiny app in the middle.

You can do this by taking advantage of the stopApp() command which is available in the latest version of shiny (but perhaps not the version on CRAN). (try `library(devtools); install_github("shiny", "rstudio")`.

stopApp accepts one argument which then gets returned from "runApp()". That would allow you to run some computationally intensive script first, get a result out of runApp(), then continue your script.

Here's an example (that uses knitr to produce an R markdown file) https://gist.github.com/trestletech/5948876 . You could, of course, just use a normal R script instead of knitting together an R markdown doc.

Jeff

> If I understand your problem correctly, I think your best bet is to wrap up your workflow in a normal R script, then interject the Shiny app in the middle.
>
> You can do this by taking advantage of the stopApp() command which is available in the latest version of shiny (but perhaps not the version on CRAN). (try `library(devtools); install_github("shiny", "rstudio")`.
>
> stopApp accepts one argument which then gets returned from "runApp()". That would allow you to run some computationally intensive script first, get a result out of runApp(), then continue your script.
>
> Here's an example (that uses knitr to produce an R markdown file) https://gist.github.com/trestletech/5948876 . You could, of course, just use a normal R script instead of knitting together an R markdown doc.

> > If you start a Shiny app from within a longer R script, is there a way to exit from the Shiny app and continue with the execution of the calling script?

> > What I am trying to do is 1) load and reformat a large dataset with an R script, 2) do some processing interactively with Shiny (low-pass filtering, baseline adjustment, peak finding), and 3) run the final computations non-interactively. That's a bit klutzy, and all the file I/O takes a while.

> > Thanks for any help,
> >
> > Richard

messages.subject: Shared UI between clients
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

after some words with Joe few days ago, here is a working demo of a shared UI between different clients (say browsers) :

ui.R
=====================
library(shiny)

shinyUI(pageWithSidebar(
  headerPanel("Shared session"),
  sidebarPanel(),

  mainPanel(
    uiOutput("slider")
  )
))

server.R
=====================
value <<- reactiveValues(v=5)

shinyServer(function(input, output, session) {

    id = floor(1000*runif(1))

    observe({
        cat(id)
        cat(".\n")
        value$v <- input$slider
    })

    output$slider <- renderUI({
        cat(id)
        cat("x\n")
        if(is.numeric(value$v)) v=value$v else v=5
        return(sliderInput("slider",label="",min=0,max=10, value=v))
    })

})

...reactive programming is amazing !

Thank you a lot Joe !

Yann

messages.subject: Re: Shiny Server, Microsoft ODBC Driver for SQL Server on Linux, and RODBC problem
messages.subject_clean: Shiny Server, Microsoft ODBC Driver for SQL Server on Linux, and RODBC problem
messages.body_plain:
I don't know about MS driver, but with FreeTDS is as follow (on CENTOS 6):

A good tuto is in http://www.webdbtips.com/256373/
- install unixODBC
    + su root
    + yum install unixODBC unixODBC-devel libtool-ltdl libtool-ltdl-devel
- install FreeTDS
    + yum install freetds
- Configure /etc/odbcinst.ini
    + nano /etc/odbcinst.ini
    + add in the end (without spaces or tabs):
# Driver for conect to MSSQL
[FreeTDS]
Description = ODBC for Microsoft SQL
Driver      = /usr/lib/libtdsodbc.so.0 # (here, you must search this file first, sometimes the file is "libtdsodbc.so", and in a 64bit sistem you must go to /usr/lib64/)
UsageCount  = 1
Threading   = 2
- Verify that the system "see" the dirve [FreeTDS]
    + odbcinst -q -d
    + The result must contain the line: [FreeTDS]
- Configure /etc/odbc.ini
    + nano /etc/odbc.ini
    + Add to the end (without spaces or tabs):
[FreeTDS-YourDataBase]
Description     = MS SQL connection to 'NDWH' database
Driver          = FreeTDS
Database        = YourDataBase
ServerName    = Name_for_YourServerName
Trace           = No

- Configure /etc/freetds.conf
    + nano /etc/freetds.conf
    + agregar al final:
# Server Name_for_YourServerName, type Microsoft SQL Server
[Name_for_YourServerName]
        host = 192.168.123.123 (The IP of your server)
        port = 1433 (the port, usually is 1433)
        tds version = 8.0 (the FreeTDS protocolo version, you could try 7.0 too)

- Verify that you could connect to the DDBB through isql
    + isql -v FreeTDS-YourDataBase user pass
    + do a query on it !!
    + If you couldn't connetc, inspect odbc.ini and odbcinst.ini
- Verify that you could connect to the DDBB through tsql
    + tsql -S Name_for_YourServerName -U user -P pass -D dataBase
    + If you have success with tsql but haven't with isql, then there are some problem in the odbc.ini or odbcinst.ini
    + If you don´t have success with tsql so you probably have a problem with the freetds.conf , tds-version , port or some configuration on the MS-SQL server

See http://freetds.schemamania.org/userguide/confirminstall.htm

El viernes, 28 de junio de 2013 21:44:34 UTC-5, Frans van Dunné escribió:
> In response to the OP: you have most likely not set up your odbc.ini properly. See below. I add further details because you may also have a unixodbc version issue (it must be 2.3) - but you did not specify.
>
> The MS ODBC drivers have just been updated to version 11 (quite a jump from 1.0, but there it is). Installing it on Ubuntu works if you take the pointers from Andrew K <http://onefinepub.com/2013/03/07/ms-sql-odbc-ubuntu/> into account. Between that post and the Microsoft documentation all steps are well described. I will summarize my steps below for Ubuntu 12.04:
>
> Download from msdn <http://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/hh568451%28v=SQL.110%29.aspx> and untar : msodbcsql-11.0.2270.0.tar.gz
>
> Make sure you have all dependencies installed: sudo apt-get install libssl1.0.0 libkrb5-3 glibc-2.13-1 e2fsprogs openssl libkrb5-3
>
> Also check that you have wget (sudo apt-get install wget).
>
> To update you unixodbc version (through the repositories you will have an older version installed) run the command as sudo bash build_dm.sh. I have no clue why it does not seem to work with the ./ prefix, for some reason I need to give the full reference to bash. The installer gives further instructions to make install unixodbc 2.3.
>
> Now install the actual driver: sudo bash install.sh install --accept-license --force
>
> the --force flag is important because otherwise it will complain that there is no rpm installed on the system (which there is not on Ubuntu). This was a tip from Andrew K again.
>
> The installer updated the /etc/odbcinst.ini file to include the driver like so it should now include:
>
> [ODBC Driver 11 for SQL Server]
> Description=Microsoft ODBC Driver 11 for SQL Server
> Driver=/opt/microsoft/msodbcsql/lib64/libmsodbcsql-11.0.so.2270.0
> Threading=1
> UsageCount=2
>
> Seeing this is a check that installation went through correctly.
>
> Now another tip from onefinepub <http://onefinepub.com/2013/03/07/ms-sql-odbc-ubuntu/> is required otherwise it will not work:
> sudo ln -s /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcrypto.so.1.0.0 /usr/lib/libcrypto.so.10
> sudo ln -s /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libssl.so.1.0.0 /usr/lib/libssl.so.10
>
> Now make sure that you configure you odbc.ini to make a DSN that connects using the new driver. It will contain the following:
>
> [ConnectionName]
> Driver       = ODBC Driver 11 for SQL Server
> Description  = ODBC connection to MSSQL Database via the Microsoft Driver
> Trace        = No
> Server       = xxx
> Servername   = xxxx
> Database     = xxx
> Trace           = No
>
> But it will not contain a username and password. You will have to pass that through to the database server when making the connection (see this post <http://social.technet.microsoft.com/Forums/sqlserver/en-US/d4eab3b3-6254-4644-a1e4-e6866f7507fd/uid-in-odbcini>).
>
> Having done all this your R will look like:
>
> > library(RODBC)
> > sqlconnection <- odbcConnect(dsn="DBNAME", uid="UserName", pwd="Pass")
>
> And your connection should be open.

messages.subject: Re: bootstrap
messages.body_plain: We are generally lacking in documentation of ways to write ui.R but here is an example of using Bootstrap: shinyUI(bootstrapPage( tags$div(class="container", tags$div(class="span6", "Hello"), tags$div(class="span6", "Goodbye") ) )) You can generate any HTML tag by calling tags$tagname as a function, where the named arguments become attributes and unnamed arguments become children. The children can be other tag$tagname calls, strings (which are then HTML-escaped), unescaped HTML strings (like this: HTML("This is bold text") ), and lists containing any of the above (and other lists). If you get tired of typing "tags$" all the time, check out the withTags function. There is also includeHTML, includeScript, includeCSS, and includeText which can also be mixed in with the above. messages.subject: Re: Shiny Server authentication?
messages.body_plain:
No - not really.
You may try it on your own. Just register for Amazon EC2 and get a micro instance for free (for 1 year).

Login to EC2 and follow this link:
https://console.aws.amazon.com/ec2/home?region=eu-west-1#launchAmi=ami-a77768d3
An new instance is created:
Continue with the first screen
Select t1.micro (the standard) or a stronger but more expensive 'hardware' and continue
Kernel ID: aki-71665e05 (this is important for XEN because I updated the kernel) and continue
Continue till the Key-Creation --> you will need the created .pem file to login using SSH
Security: you will need TCP Port 22 (SSH), 3838 (Shiny) and 8787 (RStudio)
Launch :)
After the instance started you have to start shiny. Connect with SSH and type
sudo start shiny-server

Now you can to visit the website
<your-instance-public-dns>:3838

user: test
pass: test
(can be changed at runtime in /usr/lib/node_modules/shiny-server/lib/proxy/users.htpasswd using the tool htpasswd)

You will find all standard shiny examples working including the described login-hack. In most of them the username from login is displayed in the sites header. The server includes
R 3 with openblas
RStudio
shiny
some other nice packages

ToDos:
HTTPS proxy for RStudio and Shiny using nginx (a necessary patch is already included).

--
all the best
FloE
